final.memo:
We have reviewed the business and decided to pass. We do not participate in turnarounds, particularly those requiring massive capital outlays without a clear path to durable, predictable owner earnings [D01, D08]. The Company is currently struggling with manufacturing execution and a competitive landscape that makes it difficult to assess its long-term viability [D01, D05].

When we buy a business, we look for a durable competitive advantage and a consistent record of high returns on capital [D08]. Here, the company reported a GAAP net loss of $1.6 billion and has suspended its dividend to preserve liquidity [D01]. Such financial strain is incompatible with the type of wonderful, cash-generative businesses we seek to own [D01, D08].

Capital allocation is a vital aspect of management's job [D08]. While management is currently focused on survival through cost-cutting, we prefer businesses where capital can be deployed for growth, not simply to fix fundamental manufacturing issues or maintain a precarious market position [D01, D07].

At this time, there is no margin of safety for an investor, as the company is loss-making and facing significant technological risks [D01, D02]. We find it far more prudent to hold our cash in Treasury bills, which offer certainty, rather than risking permanent capital loss on a business that has yet to prove its turnaround can succeed [D01, D08].
